title: The Letter of Windrow House
premise: When a stranger's corpse is found on the marsh road dressed in clothes stolen from Kestrel Amberdale's own closet, the retired detective realizes the killer is staging a message meant for her alone. The victim carried half of an old accounting ledger from Windrow House, the estate where, twenty years ago, Kestrel buried her testimony to protect the town's beloved matriarch. As the anniversary dinner approaches and the town's founding families close ranks, Kestrel must decode the ledger's cipher with help from her ragtag bookshop regulars—a found family she never intended to make. In the end, she exposes the decades-old murder that built Windrow House's fortune, chooses public justice over her own safety, and finally stops hiding behind alphabetized shelves.
about_author: Xanthe Halloran is the pen name of a former archivist who spent fifteen years cataloging estate papers in the English countryside before turning to crime fiction. She writes mysteries about small towns where the past is never as neatly filed as it appears.

chapters.title: The Body in Borrowed Clothes
chapters.summary: Kestrel Amberdale opens her failing bookshop on a gray morning and is summoned to the marsh road, where Constable Idris Peake shows her a dead man wearing her own missing tweed coat. Her POV establishes dread: someone knows her. Emotional beat: cold recognition that invisibility has failed.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Quiet
chapters.summary: Flashback woven through present-day inventory work reveals Kestrel's retirement from the county force after the unsolved death of young maid Tamsin Reed at Windrow House. POV alternates to Constable Peake, who suspects the coat is no coincidence. Beat: guilt resurfacing like water damage.

chapters.title: The Ledger's First Page
chapters.summary: Searching the victim's effects, Kestrel finds a torn ledger page coded in columns of dates and initials—entries matching the year of Tamsin's death. She recognizes the handwriting of housekeeper Mrs. Vane. Beat: the past has a paper trail, and it's in her hands now.

chapters.title: Regulars and Suspects
chapters.summary: Kestrel's bookshop circle—teen runaway Wren, widowed accountant Mr. Osei, gossip-loving Mrs. Fitch—each react to the murder news, revealing town loyalties. POV shifts among them. Beat: the found family assembles without knowing what they're joining.

chapters.title: Windrow House Extends an Invitation
chapters.summary: Aristocrat Edmund Windrow arrives at the shop with charm and menace, inviting Kestrel to the estate's fortieth anniversary dinner. He mentions her coat. Beat: the predator testing the door latch.

chapters.title: What Mrs. Fitch Remembers
chapters.summary: Mrs. Fitch, once a kitchen girl at Windrow House, recalls Tamsin's fear of someone 'who counted everything.' Kestrel realizes the ledger records payments—hush money or blackmail. Beat: memory as evidence.

chapters.title: The Cipher in the Columns
chapters.summary: Mr. Osei identifies the ledger's numeric pattern as a book cipher keyed to a specific volume. Kestrel searches her own shelves and finds the key text: a first edition donated years ago by the Windrows themselves. Beat: the answer was alphabetized all along.

chapters.title: Decoded: Names and Numbers
chapters.summary: The decoded entries reveal recurring payments to 'E.W.' and a final entry dated the night Tamsin died, initialed by matriarch Agatha Windrow. Kestrel's POV cracks under the weight: the woman she protected was complicit. Beat: betrayal by a ghost.

chapters.title: Wren Follows Someone
chapters.summary: Wren, tailing a suspicious visitor to the shop, witnesses a break-in at Kestrel's flat—the second half of the ledger is gone. She photographs the intruder's car. Beat: the youngest member proves braver than the adults.

chapters.title: Peake's Dilemma
chapters.summary: Constable Peake is pressured by his superiors to close the case as vagrancy-related. His POV shows institutional rot mirroring the theme of corrupted power. He quietly passes Kestrel the coroner's report: the victim was poisoned. Beat: one honest man inside a crooked system.

chapters.title: The Victim Has a Name
chapters.summary: Kestrel identifies the dead man as Silas Crane, former groundskeeper at Windrow House and Mrs. Vane's brother-in-law. He'd been blackmailing the family for years. Beat: sympathy for a blackmailer complicates the moral picture.

chapters.title: Anniversary Preparations
chapters.summary: The town prepares for the Windrow anniversary gala; invitations, menus, old grievances. Kestrel receives an anonymous note: 'Bring the page or wear the coat again.' Beat: the trap closing with polite ribbon.

chapters.title: Mrs. Vane's Deathbed Letter
chapters.summary: Kestrel tracks down the dying housekeeper's daughter, who surrenders a letter explaining Vane kept the ledger as insurance against the Windrows—and that Tamsin discovered Agatha embezzling the estate blind. Beat: motive revealed; the murder wasn't passion but arithmetic.

chapters.title: Edmund's Countermove
chapters.summary: Edmund has Kestrel's shop lease revoked and spreads rumors about her disgraced police exit. Her allies rally: Osei offers his savings, Wren organizes customers. Beat: the found family hardens into a siege garrison.

chapters.title: The Second Body
chapters.summary: Silas's contact, a local solicitor, is found drowned—dressed, again, in clothes taken from another person's closet. The staging confirms the killer is still sending messages. Beat: escalation; the pattern demands a reader.

chapters.title: Reading the Killer's Grammar
chapters.summary: Kestrel analyzes both stagings: each outfit belonged to someone who witnessed something twenty years ago. The killer isn't framing witnesses—they're dressing the dead as the guilty. Beat: the terrible clarity of understanding too late.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Dinner
chapters.summary: Kestrel reconstructs the full chain: Agatha ordered Tamsin's death; young Edmund helped conceal it; Silas and Vane profited from silence. Now someone is executing survivors one by one before the truth surfaces. Beat: dread crystallizes into resolve.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Dinner
chapters.summary: Kestrel attends the gala carrying the decoded ledger, flanked by Wren, Osei, and Peake. Toasts are raised; she stands and reads the final entry aloud. Beat: the climax—truth spoken over crystal glasses.

chapters.title: Who Counts Everything
chapters.summary: The killer is revealed: the estate's elderly accountant, Tamsin's secret father, executing his private justice before age took him. He confesses calmly, having wanted an audience all along. Beat: justice outside the law meets its mirror image.

chapters.title: Aftermath in the Shop
chapters.summary: Arrests ripple through the founding families; Peake files the full report against pressure. Kestrel reopens the shop to a line of townspeople who finally see her clearly. Beat: exhaustion and unexpected belonging.

chapters.title: What Kestrel Buries Now
chapters.summary: Kestrel visits Tamsin's unmarked grave with flowers and the original ledger page, leaving a copy with Peake for the record. She forgives herself imperfectly. Beat: grief given a place to rest.

chapters.title: Alphabetized, At Last
chapters.summary: Months later, the bookshop thrives; Wren is enrolled in school, Osei keeps the accounts, Mrs. Fitch tells everyone everything. A new customer brings a mystery, and Kestrel—no longer invisible—says yes. Beat: the found family complete, the next story knocking.
